doc_description: Netflix, Inc.’s Annual Report on Form 10‑K for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2017 (NASDAQ: NFLX; filed Jan. 29, 2018) covering its 117M‑member global streaming business and three segments (Domestic Streaming, International Streaming, Domestic DVD), 2017 results ($11.69B revenue, $559M net income, $(2.02)B free cash flow), balance sheet highlights ($14.68B content assets, $17.7B content obligations, $6.5B long‑term debt), and key risks including competition, piracy, net neutrality, AWS reliance, and foreign exchange exposure.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
- Filing overview: Netflix, Inc.’s Annual Report on Form 10-K for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2017 (Commission File No. 001-35727), filed with the U.S. SEC.
- Registrant details: Delaware corporation, EIN 77-0467272, principal offices at 100 Winchester Circle, Los Gatos, CA 95032; phone (408) 540-3700; common stock listed on NASDAQ Global Select Market.
- Filing status and compliance: Well-known seasoned issuer; large accelerated filer; compliant with reporting and interactive data file requirements; not a shell company; not an emerging growth company.
- Equity and market data: Aggregate market value of non-affiliate-held shares as of June 30, 2017: approximately $54.9 billion; shares outstanding as of January 25, 2018: 433,948,461.
- Incorporation by reference: Portions of the 2018 Proxy Statement incorporated into Part III.
- Table of contents highlights: Standard 10-K sections including Business; Risk Factors; Properties; Legal Proceedings; Market for Common Equity; Selected Financial Data; MD&A; Market Risk; Financial Statements; Controls and Procedures; and governance, compensation, ownership, related-party, and auditor fee disclosures.
- Forward-looking statements: Cautions regarding projections and expectations on strategy; operating income/margins; DVD segment decline; seasonality; contribution margins/profits; liquidity and free cash flow; revenues, net income, profitability; stock price volatility; pricing; accounting standards impacts; competitive actions; membership growth; partnerships; content agreements and viewing patterns; dividends; capital raising and debt usage; future obligations; content/marketing and original programming investments; amortization; contractual obligations; tax matters including the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, deferred tax assets, transition tax, and unrecognized tax benefits; with risks detailed in Item 1A.
- Business overview (“About Us”): Netflix describes itself as the world’s leading internet television network with over 117 million streaming memberships in more than 190 countries, streaming over 140 million hours per day; ad-free, on-demand viewing across internet-connected devices; offline downloads available; U.S. DVD-by-mail service continues.
- Strategy and operations: Core strategy to grow global streaming memberships within profit margin targets by expanding and optimizing content (including a growing slate of exclusive and original, often award-winning, programming), enhancing user interface, and broadening device reach. Streaming service launched in 2007; extensive international expansion beginning in 2010 (Canada) to near-global coverage excluding China and restricted territories.
- Business segments: Three reportable segments—Domestic Streaming, International Streaming, and Domestic DVD—each deriving revenue primarily from monthly membership fees; cross-references provided to segment financial disclosures (Note 11) in the financial statements.

- About Us: Netflix described as a leading internet television network with 117+ million streaming memberships in 190+ countries, delivering 140+ million hours of viewing per day; ad-free, on-demand viewing across internet-connected devices with pause/resume and offline downloads; U.S. members can also receive DVDs by mail.
- History and expansion: streaming launched in 2007; international expansion began in 2010 (Canada) and now largely global except China and restricted territories.
- Strategy: grow global streaming membership within profit margin targets; expand and emphasize exclusive and original programming (including self-produced, award-winning titles); enhance user interface and increase device reach.

structure.title: Business
structure.heading: Item 1. Business
structure.start_phrase:
Netflix, Inc. (“Netflix
”, “the Company”, “we”, or “us”) is the world’s leading internet television network with over 117 million streaming memberships inover 
190 countries enjoying more than 140 million hours of TV shows and movies per day, including original series, documentaries and feature films.
structure.summary:
- Forward-looking statements: outlines numerous projections and assumptions (strategy, revenues, margins, cash flows, taxes, content spend, competition, membership growth, financing) and warns of risks; references Item 1A Risk Factors; no obligation to update.
- Company overview: Netflix is a leading internet TV network with 117M streaming memberships in 190+ countries (as of 2017), offering ad-free, on-demand viewing across devices, plus a U.S. DVD-by-mail service; launched streaming in 2007.
- Strategy: grow global streaming within profit margin targets by expanding and curating content (with increasing original and exclusive programming), enhancing the user interface, extending device reach, and enabling offline downloads.
- Global expansion: began in 2010 (Canada) and now nearly worldwide except China and restricted territories; original content includes award-winning series, films, and documentaries; increasing in-house production.
- Business segments: Domestic Streaming, International Streaming, and Domestic DVD; all derive revenues from monthly membership fees; segment details cross-referenced to financial statements.
- Competition: intense and rapidly evolving against MVPDs, internet content providers (including piracy), video gaming, DVD retailers, and other entertainment options; also competes for licensed and original content; focus on “winning moments of truth” via superior technology and curated, often exclusive, content.
- Seasonality: strongest membership growth typically in Q1 and Q4; increasingly influenced by major original releases; expect more predictable seasonality as markets mature.
- Intellectual property: relies on patents, trademarks, copyrights, trade secrets, and agreements; acknowledges risks and potential disputes with no assurance of prevailing.
- Employees: approximately 5,500 total employees as of Dec 31, 2017 (about 5,400 full-time, including ~600 categorized as temporary).
- Corporate and investor information: incorporated in Delaware (1997), IPO in 2002; HQ in Los Gatos, CA; SEC filings available on website; uses IR site, SEC filings, press releases, calls, webcasts, and social media for material disclosures.
- Key risk factors highlighted: challenges in attracting/retaining members due to perceived value, pricing/feature/content changes, and churn drivers; competitive threats including piracy and well-resourced rivals; potential need for higher marketing spend to offset cancellations.
- Content commitment risks: multi-year, largely fixed-cost licensing and production (including talent) obligations not tied to usage or membership levels may constrain flexibility and adversely affect liquidity and results.

structure.title: Risk Factors
structure.heading: Item 1A. Risk Factors
structure.start_phrase:
If any of the following risks ac
tually occur, our business, financial condition and results of operations could be harmed.
structure.summary:
- This section is Item 1A: Risk Factors from an annual report, outlining threats that could harm the company’s business, financial condition, operating results, liquidity, and stock price.
- Membership growth and retention risks: impact of content quality/mix, pricing and features, competition, perceived value, word-of-mouth, and potential need for higher marketing spend if churn rises.
- Competitive pressures and piracy: fast-changing video market with strong incumbents and new entrants; aggressive pricing and content spending by competitors; piracy’s rapid global adoption and compelling “free” proposition.
- Long-term, largely fixed content commitments: multi-year licensing and production obligations with upfront cash needs; limited flexibility if growth underperforms; margin and liquidity pressure if titles underperform or can’t be shown in a territory.
- Content creation and liability risks: legal exposure (copyright, trademark, negligence), production risks (cost overruns, guild issues, key talent), brand impacts from poorly received or controversial originals, and merchandise-related liabilities.
- Licensing/rights constraints: potential refusal or withdrawal of rights by studios and other holders; rising programming costs; need for selective, often exclusive, rights; music/CMO licensing disputes and possible injunctions or litigation.
- Managing growth and complexity: global expansion, localization, regulatory variance, cloud scaling, and building original content capabilities; operational challenges if systems and practices don’t evolve effectively.
- International risks: cultural/language adaptation, staffing, management distraction, political/economic instability, compliance (FCPA, sanctions, export controls), local regulation/censorship, weaker IP laws, tax changes, FX volatility (unhedged), repatriation limits, varying payments infrastructure, piracy norms, and broadband availability.
- Tax risks: complex multi-jurisdictional tax positions under scrutiny; impacts from U.S. tax reform and potential global tax law changes that could increase taxes.
- Brand/reputation risks: negative perception of content quality or offensiveness, regulatory retaliation, ineffective marketing/PR, and challenges establishing reputation in new markets.
- Marketing and acquisition channels: changing tactics and costs; reliance on third parties that may see conflicts or favor competitors; inefficiency in content promotion could hurt acquisition/retention.
- Device and distribution partner dependence: availability, renewal terms, placement/prominence on devices and set-top boxes; device performance reflecting on the service; need for partners to update devices for tech changes.
- Technology and cybersecurity: outages (natural disasters, power/telecom failures), internet disruptions, cyber-attacks leading to service degradation, data loss, or IP theft; reliance on third-party hosting, cloud, and CDNs.
- Heavy reliance on Amazon Web Services: difficult to switch providers; AWS disruption would adversely impact operations despite Amazon’s retail business competing with the company.
- Technology performance risks: CDN interconnection with ISPs; efficacy of recommendation/merchandising systems; third-party tech or software bugs affecting operations and member devices.
- Regulatory environment: evolving rules for internet/broadcast/consumer protection and tax; net neutrality uncertainty enabling discriminatory or usage-based network practices that could raise costs or impede growth.
- ISP/network operator behavior: potential blocking, throttling, bandwidth caps, paid tiers, or preferential treatment for operators’ own video services harming service quality and growth.
- Privacy and data protection: restrictions on data collection/use, localization/export mandates; breach risks for member/employee data with legal, financial, and reputational impacts; limited insurance coverage.
- Payment processing risks: disruptions, rising fees, ecosystem changes, partner billing reliance, rules/regulatory changes, and fraud impacting revenue, expenses, and acquisition/retention.
- Intellectual property protection and disputes: challenges enforcing trademarks, patents, trade secrets, and domains; costly IP litigation and potential need for licenses, workarounds, or content removal.
- Legal proceedings: increasing litigation (copyright, patents, consumer, securities) causing unforeseen costs, management distraction, and possible content/service disruptions.
- Capital needs and leverage: negative operating cash flows due to content investment; potential capital raises causing dilution or senior securities; substantial debt and significant on- and off-balance-sheet content obligations.
- Debt service and liquidity risks: potential inability to generate sufficient cash; need to refinance/restructure at worse terms; possible asset sales or reduced investments; material adverse effects if alternatives fail.
- Talent risks: dependence on CEO and key leaders; competitive market for skilled personnel, with recruitment/retention challenges.
- Domestic DVD segment decline: faster-than-expected shrinkage or service issues could reduce contribution profit; USPS rate hikes or service reductions could further hurt profitability.
- Stock ownership and market risks: anti-takeover charter provisions and Delaware law; executive retention payments upon change-in-control; stock price volatility; potential for securities litigation; forecasting/estimation errors (e.g., content amortization) could lead to misses and stock declines.

structure.title: Selected Financial Data
structure.heading: Item 6. Selected Financial Data
structure.start_phrase:
The following selected consol
idated financial data is not necessarily indicative of results of future operations and should be read in conjunction with Item 7,"Management’s Discussion and Analysis o
f Financial Condition and Results of Operations" and Item 8, "Financial Statements and Supplementary Data."
structure.summary:
- Scope: Excerpts from Netflix’s 2017 Form 10-K covering Item 6 (Selected Financial Data) and the opening of Item 7 (MD&A), with EPS/share counts adjusted for the July 2015 seven-for-one stock split (see Note 7).
- Consolidated results (2013–2017):
  - Strong top-line growth: revenues rose from $4.37B (2013) to $11.69B (2017).
  - Profitability improved: operating income from $228M to $839M; net income from $112M to $559M.
  - EPS increased (basic $0.28 to $1.29; diluted $0.26 to $1.25). Weighted-average diluted shares grew from ~425M to ~447M.
- Cash flows and liquidity:
  - Operating cash flow turned negative in 2015–2017 (e.g., $(1.79)B in 2017).
  - Free cash flow negative and widening (e.g., $(2.02)B in 2017); defined as net cash from operating and investing activities excluding movements in short-term investments; reconciliation referenced in Liquidity and Capital Resources.
- Balance sheet trends:
  - Cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments: $1.20B (2013) to $2.82B (2017).
  - Total content assets (net) expanded sharply: $3.84B to $14.68B; total content liabilities: $3.12B to $7.50B.
  - Long-term debt increased to fund content and growth: $0.49B to $6.50B.
  - Total assets rose to $19.0B; stockholders’ equity to $3.58B.
- Operating metrics:
  - Global streaming memberships grew from 44.4M (2013) to 117.6M (2017); 2017 net additions of 23.8M.
  - Membership definition includes free trials with a payment method; cancellations effective at period end (voluntary) or immediately upon failed payment (involuntary).
- 2017 MD&A highlights vs. 2016:
  - Revenues +32%; operating income +121%; net income +199%; operating margin up from 4% to 7%.
  - Global average monthly revenue per paying membership up 10% to $9.43.
  - International revenue share rose to 44% (from 36%); average paid international memberships were 49% of total (from 43%).
  - Growth drivers: higher paid memberships (especially international), pricing adjustments, and plan mix.
- Costs and other items:
  - Higher content expenses from acquiring/licensing/producing content, including a $39.1M expense for abandoned unreleased content; increased headcount to support service improvements, international expansion, and production.
  - Net income aided by tax benefit from adoption of ASU 2016-09; partially offset by higher interest expense (more notes outstanding) and FX losses (euro-denominated notes remeasurement).
- Pricing and plans:
  - Three streaming plans: Basic (SD, 1 screen), Standard (HD, 2 screens), Premium (HD/UHD, 4 screens).
  - 2017 pricing: U.S. $7.99–$13.99/month; international roughly $4–$20/month; prices may rise over time by market.
- Segment reporting and cost structure:
  - Contribution profit defined as segment revenues less cost of revenues and marketing; used to assess segment performance, with growing emphasis on global operating margin as international markets mature.
  - Cost of revenues largely driven by amortization of streaming content assets; multi-territory/global rights allocated between Domestic and International based on estimated fair value.
  - Other costs include content acquisition/licensing/production and streaming delivery; Netflix’s Open Connect CDN and third-party delivery costs are included.

structure.title: Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.heading: Item 7. Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations
structure.start_phrase:
The following represents our conso
lidated performance highlights:
structure.summary:
- Document type and scope: Management’s Discussion and Analysis (MD&A), Item 7/7A of an annual report, covering consolidated results, segment performance (Domestic Streaming, International Streaming, Domestic DVD), operating expenses, liquidity/capital resources, contractual obligations, critical accounting policies, and market risk for years ended December 31, 2017, 2016, and 2015.

- Consolidated highlights (2017 vs. 2016):
  - Global streaming memberships: 117.6M (up 25%).
  - Average monthly revenue per paying membership: $9.43 (up 10%).
  - Revenues: $11.69B (up 32%); International revenue 44% of total (vs. 36%).
  - Operating income: $838.7M (up 121%); operating margin 7% (from 4%).
  - Net income: $558.9M (up 199%).
  - Growth drivers: larger global paid member base (notably international), higher ARPU from price changes and plan mix; partially offset by higher content costs (including $39.1M for abandoned unreleased content), higher headcount costs, and FX losses (euro note remeasurement).

- Service and pricing:
  - Three streaming plans (Basic/Standard/Premium) with varying video quality and concurrent streams.
  - 2017 pricing: U.S. $7.99–$13.99; international roughly $4–$20 equivalent; prices may increase over time.

- Segment results:
  - Domestic Streaming:
    - 2017 year-end memberships: 54.8M; paid 52.8M; net adds 5.3M.
    - ARPU: $10.18 (up 11%).
    - Revenues: $6.15B (up 21%).
    - Contribution margin: 37% (up from 36%).
    - Cost increases driven by content amortization and other operating costs (payment processing, customer service); marketing spend up; expectation that 2018 marketing growth will outpace revenue growth.
  - International Streaming:
    - 2017 year-end memberships: 62.8M; paid 57.8M; net adds 18.5M.
    - ARPU: $8.66 (up 11%).
    - Revenues: $5.09B (up 58%); FX tailwind ~ $21.9M vs. 2016 rates.
    - Contribution margin: 4% (vs. -10% in 2016); profitability in mature markets offsetting newer market investments.
    - Costs up due to content amortization and delivery/customer service/payment fees; marketing increased.
  - Domestic DVD:
    - Continuing decline in memberships (3.38M at year-end 2017).
    - Revenues fell to $450.5M; contribution margin improved to 55% due to lower usage and content costs.

- Operating expenses (consolidated):
  - Technology & Development: $1.05B (9% of revenue), up due to headcount, cloud costs, and facilities (expanded Los Gatos HQ).
  - General & Administrative: $863.6M (7% of revenue), up due to higher headcount supporting international expansion and original content production, facilities expansion (Los Gatos and Los Angeles), and third-party services.

- Interest and other income/expense:
  - Interest expense: $238.2M (up 59%) due to higher long-term debt.
  - Interest and other income (expense): $(115.2)M driven by $127.9M FX loss, primarily from remeasurement of €1.3B senior notes.

- Taxes:
  - 2017 effective tax rate: -15% (benefit), reflecting excess tax benefits from stock-based compensation (ASU 2016-09), corporate restructuring that increased foreign income at lower tax rates, and R&D credits; partially offset by state taxes and non-deductibles.
  - Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (2017): provisional $79.1M tax expense (deferred tax remeasurement $46.9M; transition tax $32.2M on $484.9M cumulative foreign earnings); $66.5M benefit from foreign taxes expensed in prior years now creditable. SAB 118 applied; further adjustments expected in 2018.

- Liquidity and capital resources:
  - Cash and short-term investments: $2.82B; foreign cash $611.3M.
  - Long-term debt: $6.50B (up from $3.36B) after issuing €1.3B notes (May 2017) and $1.6B notes (Oct 2017); earliest maturity 2021.
  - $500M unsecured revolving credit facility (plus $250M accordion); undrawn at year-end.
  - Strategy to finance capital needs in debt markets; equity could be dilutive.
  - Negative free cash flow expected for many years due to upfront investments in owned/original content; 2017 FCF $(2.02)B vs. net income due mainly to excess cash content payments over amortization.

- Cash flows (2017):
  - Operating activities: $(1.79)B (higher content cash spend; higher operating costs; partially offset by revenue growth).
  - Investing activities: +$34.3M (higher capex offset by net sales/maturities of short-term investments and lower DVD spend).
  - Financing activities: +$3.08B (net proceeds from 2017 note issuances).

- Contractual obligations (as of 12/31/2017):
  - Total: $28.0B.
  - Streaming content obligations: $17.7B (includes $7.5B due <1 year); $10.2B not on balance sheet yet; additional $3–$5B estimated for unknown future titles over next three years.
  - Debt (principal + interest): $9.05B.
  - Lease obligations: $737.4M (HQ and office facilities).
  - Other purchase obligations: $544.9M.
  - Unrecognized tax benefits: $42.9M (timing of resolution uncertain).

- Off-balance sheet arrangements: None (no SPEs/structured finance exposures).

- Indemnifications: As disclosed in financial statement notes.

- Critical accounting policies and estimates:
  - Streaming content: capitalization and accelerated amortization based on viewing patterns and availability window; significant judgment in estimating use; write-offs for abandoned content.
  - Income taxes: deferred tax measurement, valuation allowances, uncertain tax positions; impact and provisional accounting under the 2017 Tax Act per SAB 118.

- Market risk (Item 7A):
  - Interest rate risk: fixed-rate unsecured debt (2021–2028 maturities); fair value sensitive to rate movements.
  - Foreign currency risk: significant international revenues and costs; exposure mainly to EUR, GBP, CAD, AUD, JPY, BRL; 2017 FX increased international revenue by ~$21.9M; FX losses recognized on euro notes and remeasurement of non-functional currency balances; no hedging program in place.

structure.title: Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
structure.heading: Item 7A. Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures About Market Risk
structure.start_phrase:
We are exposed to marke
t risks related to interest rate changes and the corresponding changes in the market values of our debt and foreign currencyfluctuations.
structure.summary:
- Item 7A (Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures about Market Risk): Discusses exposure to interest rate and foreign currency risks.
- Interest rate risk: As of December 31, 2017, cash equivalents held in money market funds; all short-term investments were sold in July 2017. The company had $6.6 billion of fixed-rate unsecured debt in seven tranches due 2021–2028; the fair value of this debt fluctuates with interest rate movements and foreign exchange changes.
- Foreign currency risk: Significant international exposure (44% of revenue and 54% of cost of revenues in 2017). Key currencies include EUR, GBP, CAD, AUD, JPY, and BRL. A change in FX rates affected results: 2017 international revenues would have been about $21.9 million lower if 2016 FX rates had persisted.
- FX gains/losses: Recorded a $127.9 million foreign exchange loss in 2017, primarily from remeasurement of €1,300.0 million Senior Notes, partially offset by remeasurement of content liabilities in non-functional currencies. FX changes increased cash and cash equivalents by $29.8 million in 2017.
- Hedging: The company does not use foreign exchange contracts or derivatives to hedge currency exposures; continued international expansion increases FX sensitivity.
- Item 8 (Financial Statements and Supplementary Data): Directs to consolidated financial statements and notes included by reference in Part IV, Item 15(a)(1).
- Item 9 (Changes in and Disagreements with Accountants): None reported.

structure.summary:
- Item 7A: Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures about Market Risk
  - Interest rate risk: All short-term investments were sold in July 2017. As of December 31, 2017, cash equivalents were in money market funds with rates that float with market conditions. The company had $6.6 billion of fixed-rate unsecured debt in seven tranches due 2021–2028; the fair value of this debt moves inversely with interest rates and is also affected by foreign currency changes.
  - Foreign currency risk: In 2017, international revenues were 44% and international cost of revenues 54% of consolidated totals. Major exposure currencies include EUR, GBP, CAD, AUD, JPY, and BRL. A stronger U.S. dollar can reduce reported international revenue and contribution profit. The company estimates 2017 international revenues would have been about $21.9 million lower if 2016 FX rates had persisted. It recorded a $127.9 million foreign exchange loss primarily from remeasuring €1.3 billion in Senior Notes, partially offset by remeasurement of content liabilities; FX changes increased cash and cash equivalents by $29.8 million. The company does not use derivatives to hedge FX exposures, and growing international operations heighten FX volatility risk to future results.
- Item 8: Financial Statements and Supplementary Data—Consolidated financial statements and notes are included in Part IV, Item 15(a)(1), and incorporated by reference.
- Item 9: Changes in and Disagreements with Accountants on Accounting and Financial Disclosure—None.

- No changes occurred in ICFR during the quarter ended December 31, 2017 that materially affected, or were reasonably likely to materially affect, ICFR.

The audit was conducted under PCAOB standards, with statements on independence, scope, and the definition and inherent limitations of ICFR. EY also referenced their unqualified opinion on the consolidated financial statements for the three years ended December 31, 2017.

structure.heading: Item 15. Exhibits, Financial Statement Schedules
structure.start_phrase: The following documents are f iled as part of this Annual Report on Form 10-K:
structure.summary:
- Scope and structure: Part IV of Netflix, Inc.’s 2017 Form 10-K covering Item 15 (Exhibits, Financial Statement Schedules) and Item 16 (Form 10-K Summary—none), the full audited consolidated financial statements with notes, auditor’s reports, exhibit index, signatures, and officer certifications.

- Auditor’s opinion: Ernst & Young LLP issued unqualified opinions on the consolidated financial statements for 2015–2017 and on internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, 2017.

- Business and segments: Description of Netflix’s streaming and DVD businesses with three reportable segments—Domestic Streaming, International Streaming, and Domestic DVD. Over 117 million streaming memberships in 190+ countries.

- Financial results (2017 vs prior years):
  - Revenues: $11.69B (2016: $8.83B; 2015: $6.78B)
  - Operating income: $838.7M (2016: $379.8M; 2015: $305.8M)
  - Net income: $558.9M (2016: $186.7M; 2015: $122.6M)
  - Diluted EPS: $1.25 (2016: $0.43; 2015: $0.28)
  - Comprehensive income: $586.9M

- Cash flows and liquidity (2017):
  - Net cash used in operating activities: $(1.79)B (driven by content spend)
  - Investing activities: $34M provided
  - Financing activities: $3.08B provided (notably debt issuance)
  - Cash and cash equivalents: $2.82B at year-end (sold all short-term investments in July 2017)

- Balance sheet highlights (12/31/2017):
  - Total assets: $19.0B
  - Content assets, net: $14.68B (current $4.31B; non-current $10.37B)
  - Long-term debt: $6.50B outstanding senior unsecured notes
  - Stockholders’ equity: $3.58B

- Content accounting and obligations:
  - Capitalization and accelerated amortization of licensed and produced content based on viewing patterns; most titles amortized largely within four years.
  - Streaming content obligations: $17.7B total (payments: <1 year $7.45B; 1–3 years $8.21B; 3–5 years $1.89B; >5 years $0.14B), including $7.5B on balance sheet and $10.2B off-balance sheet (not yet meeting recognition criteria).

- Debt and credit facilities:
  - Multiple senior notes outstanding totaling $6.50B (including €1.3B 2027 notes; FX remeasurement loss recorded).
  - New $500M unsecured revolving credit facility (with $250M accordion) established July 2017; no borrowings outstanding at year-end; covenant compliant.

- Leases and facilities:
  - Significant non-cancelable operating lease commitments through 2027 (future minimum payments $737M).
  - Los Gatos HQ buildings accounted for as financing obligations due to construction funding involvement.

- Taxes:
  - Effective tax rate 2017: (15)% driven by increased foreign earnings at lower tax rates, stock-based comp excess tax benefits, and U.S. tax reform impacts.
  - Tax Cuts and Jobs Act: provisional charges of $46.9M (deferred remeasurement) and $32.2M (transition tax) recorded; $66.5M benefit for foreign tax credits; additional analysis pending under SAB 118.
  - Deferred tax assets include R&D and foreign tax credits; valuation allowance primarily on certain foreign tax credits.

- Stockholders’ equity and compensation:
  - Seven-for-one stock split effected in 2015; 4.99B authorized common shares.
  - Ongoing monthly grants of fully vested employee stock options; 2017 stock-based compensation expense $182.2M; options outstanding ~21.6M with $2.83B aggregate intrinsic value at year-end.

- Segment performance and memberships:
  - 2017 memberships at period end: Domestic Streaming 54.8M, International Streaming 62.8M, Domestic DVD 3.4M.
  - 2017 revenues: Domestic Streaming $6.15B; International Streaming $5.09B; Domestic DVD $0.45B.
  - Contribution profit 2017: Domestic Streaming $2.28B; International Streaming $0.23B; Domestic DVD $0.25B.
  - Amortization of content assets 2017: $6.26B total (Domestic $2.76B; International $3.44B; DVD $0.06B).

- Other policies and disclosures:
  - Marketing expense 2017: $1.28B; Technology and development: $1.05B; G&A: $0.86B.
  - R&D expenses included within Technology and Development ($981M in 2017).
  - Foreign currency translation and transaction effects; 2017 FX loss on debt remeasurement.
  - EPS methodology; details on options excluded from dilution when anti-dilutive.

- New accounting standards:
  - Adopted ASU 2016-09 (share-based payment) in 2017 (prospective); early adopted ASU 2017-01 (definition of a business).
  - Planned adoptions: ASC 606 revenue (Q1 2018; not material), ASC 842 leases (Q1 2019; will add right-of-use assets and lease liabilities), ASU 2016-18 restricted cash (Q1 2018; not material); GILTI accounted for as period cost beginning 2018.

- Legal, guarantees, and contingencies:
  - Routine litigation not considered material; recognition policy for contingencies explained.
  - Indemnification obligations to partners, directors, and officers; maximum exposure not reasonably estimable.

- Quarterly data (unaudited): 2016–2017 quarterly revenues, gross profit, net income, and EPS provided.

- Exhibits, signatures, and certifications:
  - Comprehensive exhibit index including indentures, purchase agreements, revolving credit agreement, compensation plans, and XBRL files.
  - List of significant subsidiaries in the U.S., Netherlands, Brazil, Japan, and Singapore.
  - EY consent; CEO/CFO Section 302 and 906 certifications; power of attorney and board/officer signatures dated January 29, 2018.
